what_it_does: When a language model generates text one token at a time (the 'decode' phase), the attention step — where the model compares the new token against every previous token in the conversation — is starved of GPU parallelism. Existing fast-attention libraries only parallelize over batch size and number of heads, leaving most of the GPU's processing cores idle during long conversations. LeanAttention fixes this by dividing the context-length work evenly across every available core, achieving close to 100% hardware occupancy and delivering up to 2.18x speedup over the previous best approach.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A GPU runs many parallel 'worker groups' (called Streaming Multiprocessors, or SMs). During token generation, attention needs to compare the new token against thousands of cached previous tokens. This workload is inherently sequential in existing libraries — each SM handles a whole head or a fixed chunk — leaving many SMs idle when the numbers don't divide evenly.

How it works. LeanAttention uses a technique called Stream-K decomposition, borrowed from fast matrix multiplication. It treats the entire attention computation as a flat list of work units called LeanTiles — each LeanTile covers a fixed block of the cached context (256 tokens on an A100 GPU for most models). It then divides these tiles equally among all available SMs, regardless of head or batch boundaries. If a tile straddles the boundary between two different 'heads,' the SM computes a partial result and hands it off.

The key design choice. Partial attention outputs from different SMs can be combined exactly because softmax re-scaling — the normalization step inside attention — is associative (like addition: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c)). LeanAttention proves this formally and uses it to reduce partial outputs from differently-sized chunks without any approximation, producing bit-exact results.

The catch. There is a small synchronization cost when one SM must wait for another to finish a partial result before it can merge, but the paper shows this overhead is under 3% in almost all practical cases.

The result. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, LeanAttention achieves an average 1.73x speedup over FlashDecoding across more than 1,000 benchmark configurations, reaching up to 2.18x for 256,000-token context lengths. On an H100 GPU it reaches 2.52x for 64k contexts. End-to-end inference speedup with a real model (Phi-3 Medium) reaches 1.73x for long outputs.
